original_question: Let {gamma_k}_{k>=0} be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers such that f(x)=sum_{k>=0} gamma_k x^k/k! is an entire function. For parameters p with -p not in N, define the generalized Bessel-type function F_p(x)=sum_{k>=0} gamma_k x^k/(k! Gamma(k+p+1)). Characterize exactly which nonnegative sequences {gamma_k} make F_p belong to the Laguerre-Polya class of real entire functions.
target_in_paper: Section 1 (Introduction), Problem 1. The draft matches the paper's introductory open problem on characterizing non-negative sequences whose generalized Bessel-type transform F_p lies in the Laguerre–Pólya class. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
correct_elements: It correctly captures the non-negative sequence hypothesis, the exponential generating function f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \gamma_k x^k/k!, the generalized Bessel-type transform F_p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \gamma_k x^k/(k!\Gamma(k+p+1)), and the goal of characterizing when that transform belongs to the Laguerre–Pólya class. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
missing_details: The paper's question is simultaneous in the parameter: one asks for F_p to belong to \mathcal{L}\!-ℙ for every admissible p, not merely for a fixed or unspecified p. The introduction writes the condition as 'for -p\notin\mathbb{N}'. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))

To make the question stand-alone, p should be stated as a real parameter p\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1,-2,\dots\}; this is implicit in the paper's focus on real entire functions in \mathcal{L}\!-ℙ. This is an inference from the surrounding context of Problem 1 and equation (1.4). ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))

The paper formulates the problem conditionally: characterize those non-negative sequences for which, whenever f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \gamma_k x^k/k! is entire, the transformed series F_p has the desired \mathcal{L}\!-ℙ property. Your draft is close, but the dependency on the entire-function hypothesis should remain explicit in the quantified statement. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))

The formal target class in Problem 1 is \mathcal{L}\!-ℙ, not the smaller class \mathcal{L}\!-ℙ^{+}; this matters because the denominator \Gamma(k+p+1) can change sign for some admissible negative nonintegral p. The draft says 'Laguerre-Polya class of real entire functions,' which is correct, but preserving this exact scope is important. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))

The nearby context explains that cases where \{\gamma_k\} is already a classical multiplier sequence are trivial positive examples, so the real interest is in non-multiplier sequences whose transformed coefficients still yield the \mathcal{L}\!-ℙ property; this is motivation rather than an extra hypothesis, but it is part of the paper-faithful intent. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
refined_question:
Let \{\gamma_k\}_{k\ge 0} be a sequence of nonnegative real numbers such that the exponential generating function
f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \gamma_k\,\frac{x^k}{k!}
is an entire function. For each real parameter p\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\{-1,-2,\dots\}, define the generalized Bessel-type entire function
F_p(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\gamma_k}{k!\,\Gamma(k+p+1)}x^k.
Characterize all such sequences \{\gamma_k\}_{k\ge 0} for which F_p belongs to the Laguerre–Pólya class \mathcal{L}\!-ℙ for every admissible p. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
justification: The draft is aiming at the paper's introductory open problem, not at the separate Section 3.1 conjectural discussion about the special function \sum_{k\ge0}\sqrt{k}\,x^k/(k!k!). The exact match is Section 1, Problem 1: it uses the same sequence hypothesis, the same transform F_p, and the same \mathcal{L}\!-ℙ membership question. The surrounding introduction then explains why generalized Bessel terminology is used via the modified Bessel function I_p in equation (1.4), and it notes that classical multiplier sequences give only the easy part of the story; Proposition 20 later supplies a concrete supporting example with quadratic polynomial data. ([sciencedirect.com](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022247X15007854?utm_source=openai))
